en: Freezing is legitimate here because you are going to melt it anyway. Slice it first, interleave with paper, and go straight from the freezer to the grill.
University of Hawaii postharvest guidance records about 3 to 5 days at 20 °C and 60% relative humidity. The spines dry and blacken first; the flesh is usually still good at that point.

Best at 8 to 15 °C with high humidity, which gives 14 to 16 days. A home refrigerator runs colder than that, so keep the fruit in a sealed bag in the least cold part and expect the shorter end of the range.

FSSAI puts rasgulla, rasmalai, sandesh, cham cham and rajbhog in the 'Short Shelf Life' class: keep refrigerated and eat within two days of the date of manufacture. The syrup does not preserve them — the ball is fresh chhena, a soft high-moisture curd. Buy from a counter with real refrigeration and note that mithai shops often sell yesterday's tray.
Scale and gut before chilling; hold at 4C or below and eat it raw only on the day it is cut.
Freezing costs the firm texture prized for sashimi - freeze only fish you plan to cook.
Unopened jars and sachets keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard.

Refrigerate once opened. Like every rempah, it is ground fresh shallot, garlic, ginger, galangal, turmeric and chilli — low-acid produce, usually sitting under oil, which is the exact combination NCHFP warns about. Five days cold is the USDA FoodKeeper figure for the equivalent Thai curry paste; NCHFP's limit for garlic in oil is four days at 4 °C or lower.
Freeze in portions. Homemade bumbu is much better frozen than refrigerated — NCHFP allows garlic in oil to be frozen 'for up to several months', and a fried-off paste keeps its flavour through it.
Ohio State Extension's pantry chart gives unopened vinegar 2 years. Cool dark cupboard, capped. Vinegar is acid — it is one of the barrier foods that does not need refrigeration at all.

Ohioline gives opened vinegar 12 months. A cloudy haze or a gelatinous blob (a vinegar 'mother') in an old bottle is harmless; strain it out or ignore it. Seasoned or sushi vinegar has sugar and salt added and will taste tired sooner than the plain kind.

米酒, Shaoxing and the other Chinese cooking wines are brewed or fortified alcohol at roughly 15 to 20 percent by volume, and alcohol at that strength is itself a preservation barrier — the FDA's labelling guidance lists barriers of this kind alongside acidification and salt as alternatives to refrigeration. Keep the bottle capped, upright, cool and dark. It does not need the fridge and does not spoil in the ordinary sense; what it does is oxidise, going flat and slightly sharp over a year or so of an open bottle. Cooking wines sold with salt added to dodge liquor licensing behave the same way.

While the fat cap is unbroken and the pot is sealed, go by the date on it — a commercially potted rillettes is dated in weeks, and the fat is what makes that possible. Keep it at or below 4 °C. Health Canada and the FDA both name refrigerated pâtés and meat spreads as a Listeria risk, and Listeria grows in the fridge, so a long-dated chilled pot is exactly the kind of food where the date matters.

Break the fat cap and you have opened the product — that is the whole point of this record. The layer of white fat on top is not decoration and not a garnish; it is an oxygen and moisture barrier over a cooked, low-acid, ready-to-eat meat, and once you dig through it the meat underneath is on the same clock as any cooked meat dish: 3 to 4 days at or below 4 °C, New Mexico State's figure. Smoothing the fat back over the surface makes it look sealed again. It is not.
Freeze it in the pot or in small ramekins with the fat layer intact. The texture survives freezing better than a smooth pâté does because the meat is already shredded.
CTAHR: harvested fruit fully ripens in 5 to 8 days. Once the skin turns fully black the pulp goes clear and mucous and the fruit is edible for only 1 or 2 more days before it ferments.
CTAHR records a shelf life of less than one week; refrigeration buys a couple of days at the ripe stage but this Annona is chilling-sensitive.

Wrap the cut face in its original foil or in waxed paper — foil is traditional here for a reason, it stops the paste drying and the blue over-breathing — then box it loosely at 0–5 °C. Roquefort is saltier and drier than gorgonzola dolce, which buys it a week or two, but it is still a moist, low-acid cheese and it goes on ripening in your fridge until it turns bitter and ammoniac.
Not recommended. It thaws into wet crumbs. Use those in a dressing if you have already done it.

Cut side down on a board under a cloth, or in a paper bag inside a bread bin. A dense sour rye is the best keeper of any bread here: it is acidic from the rye sour, and rye's pentosans hold water so it dries slowly. A sealed, sliced, dark rye pack from the supermarket keeps to its printed date and then moulds fast once opened, because the pack has been holding humidity against it.

Don't, unless you are only going to toast it. Refrigeration is the worst temperature for bread: a controlled study of storage conditions found pan wheat bread firmed to 424 % of its initial value after 10 days at 8.2 °C against 390 % at 21.9 °C. Cold does not stop staling, it accelerates it — the amylopectin side chains recrystallise fastest a little above freezing. The same study found no visible mould at 8.2 °C over 10 days, so the fridge buys you mould-freedom at the cost of texture. That is only a good trade for bread you are going to toast.

Freezing does stop staling, because the starch cannot recrystallise below the glass transition. Slice the loaf first, freeze it in a bag, toast from frozen. This is the right answer for any bread you cannot finish in a few days.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial salad dressing is safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.
Keep the scaly skin on and store dry and cool; overripe fruit turns tasteless and develops an off odour.
Loose in a paper bag rather than sealed plastic, which sweats and rots the fruit.

A whole, unopened dry-cured sausage in its natural casing hangs in a cool, dry, airy place — that is how it is sold in Spain and how it goes on drying. It gets firmer and more concentrated with time. The white bloom on the casing is the intended surface mould and is fine; fuzzy grey, green or black patches, or a sour ammonia smell, are not.

Once cut or once a vacuum pack is opened, refrigerate at or below 40 °F (4 °C). Wrap the cut end in paper rather than plastic film so it can still breathe a little, and slice from it as you go. Sliced salchichón dries out and browns within days — buy the piece, not the packet, if you are not going to finish it.
Freezing is a last resort. The fat oxidises and the texture goes crumbly; the flavour does not survive well.

Shorter than gazpacho, and for a specific reason: salmorejo is a raw emulsion and is very often made with raw egg or egg yolk to help it hold, and it is finished with chopped hard-boiled egg and jamón. Refrigerate it immediately at 4 °C, covered, and eat it the day it is made or the next. Never leave it standing at room temperature on a summer table.
Do not freeze it. The whole point of salmorejo is a stable emulsion of oil, bread and tomato, and freezing breaks it irreversibly.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial salsa is safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.

Taiwan's 食農教育資訊整合平臺 describes the cure as soaking in brine of 20 % salt or stronger at room temperature for 20 to 30 days, after which the eggs are cooked. Raw brined eggs keep in their brine in a cool dark place; once you lift them out of the brine the clock starts.
Hard-cooked salted eggs are cooked eggs — 4 °C or below, in the shell, and eat within about a week. Salted egg yolks separated for baking or for 蛋黃酥 should be used the same day or frozen.
Freeze the raw or cooked yolks, not whole eggs in the shell — the shell cracks and the white turns rubbery.

Vacuum-packed or loose yolks, raw or already baked, at 4 °C or below in a sealed box. Salt-cured they may be, but a yolk lifted out of its shell and its brine has lost most of its protection and is a rich, low-acid food. Baked or steamed yolks for 蛋黃酥 and mooncakes should go straight from cooling into the fridge and be used within the week.

The right way to keep a bag of yolks. Freeze them in a single layer then bag them; they go slightly grainy but that does not matter once they are baked into a pastry or mashed into a sauce. Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter.

Whole, hard-cured salted fish keeps wrapped in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place. Hong Kong's CFS rule for goods that need no refrigeration is a sealed or covered container somewhere cool and dry. Salt content varies enormously by style, and softer, wetter cures are not shelf-stable at all.
Wrap tightly — the smell travels — and refrigerate, which is the safer default in a warm climate and for any cure you are unsure about. Once cut, keep the pieces sealed.
Freezing stops the fat oxidising, which is what turns salted fish yellow and bitter.
The thick rind protects the fruit; keep it dry and out of the sun.
Loose in the crisper. Peeled segments should be eaten the same day.
Ripen at room temperature until it yields to a thumb. CTAHR warns that fruit picked immature shrivels as it softens and never sweetens properly.
Refrigerate only after it has softened.
Unopened vacuum or modified-atmosphere packs, refrigerated at or below 4 °C, to the printed date. Lay them flat; a pack that has puffed up has lost its seal.

This is the number that matters, and it is much shorter than people expect from a sausage that hangs happily in a cellar when whole. Slicing turns a small, dry, protected surface into a large, thin, freshly handled one — the moment where post-curing contamination and rapid oxidation both come in. Re-wrap the slices tightly touching each other and eat within a few days; they go brown, waxy and hard at the edges long before they become unsafe.
A compromise. The fat oxidises and the texture goes greasy; use thawed slices in a stew or on a pizza rather than on a board.

A whole, uncut, fully dried saucisson hangs. Somewhere cool, dry and airy — a larder, a cellar, a north-facing pantry, 12–16 °C — with air on all sides and never in a plastic bag, which sweats it. It goes on drying and hardening for as long as you leave it, which is not spoilage: eventually it is too hard to slice pleasantly, and that is the practical limit rather than a safety one. The powdery white bloom on the casing is a deliberate Penicillium culture and is normal. Fuzzy green, grey or black growth, a slimy casing, or a sour or rancid smell is not, and Hong Kong's CFS's position on visibly mouldy food is to throw it out because the hyphae go deeper than the patch.

The fridge is a fine second choice, and the right one in a warm humid climate. Wrap the sausage in paper, not plastic, so it can still lose moisture. It will dry harder and faster in there than in a cellar because a fridge is a dehumidifier.

A crock at room temperature is fermenting, not storing, and this is the only stage that belongs out of the fridge. USDA's recommendation, via NCHFP, is 70–75 °F (21–24 °C) while fermenting, where kraut is fully fermented in about 3 to 4 weeks; at 60–65 °F (15–18 °C) it takes 5 to 6 weeks; above 75 °F the kraut may go soft. Keep the cabbage under the brine the whole time and skim the surface. Do not cut back the salt — NCHFP is explicit that the salt is not seasoning, it is what favours the lactic bacteria over everything else.

Once it is fully fermented, tightly covered in the refrigerator. NCHFP says fully fermented kraut keeps 'for several months' this way, and gives 4 to 6 months for fully fermented pickles in their original container, provided they are refrigerated and surface scum and moulds are removed regularly — Ohio State gives the same 4 to 6 months. Check the jar a couple of times a week and skim. The kraut goes on souring slowly and softening; it is still fermenting, just very slowly.

Ohio State gives unopened canned foods 12 months in the pantry, and sauerkraut is a high-acid canned good, which is the easy end of canning. Cool, dark and dry. A jar with a bulging lid, a rusted or dented seam, or that hisses and smells wrong when opened goes in the bin unopened where possible.

Ohio State gives opened canned pickles and olives 1 to 2 months refrigerated, and jarred kraut keeps the same way: the acid does the work, the cold slows the yeasts and moulds that eventually grow on the surface. Keep the cabbage under its liquid and use a clean fork. This is a much longer life than the live version has — because there is nothing alive in it.
Keep the interleaving sheets between the discs and cook straight from frozen - a thawed disc turns into a sticky lump you cannot separate.
Not a fridge food. If a pack has thawed in the fridge, cook it that day rather than refreezing it.
The berries burst easily; keep them in a shallow layer and do not wash until use.
Sea buckthorn is almost always frozen straight after harvest — the berries are usually shaken off frozen branches — and juiced from frozen.

Uni is the most perishable thing in this list — raw gonad with no skin, no salt and no acid. Keep the tray at 4 °C or below on ice, do not let it sit at room temperature while you prepare anything else, and eat it the day you buy it if you possibly can. Lobes that have gone soft, weeping or bitter are past it.
Cooked seitan is a moist, low-acid, cooked protein — treat it as a leftover and keep it in its cooking broth in a sealed box at 4 °C or below. Vacuum packs keep to the printed date unopened.
Freezes well in its broth; the texture firms slightly, which most people prefer.

Airtight container in a cool cupboard. Semolina is milled from the endosperm with the germ largely removed, so it keeps like white flour rather than like a whole grain — the thing that ends it is usually insects or a musty smell from damp, not rancidity. Dry-roasting a batch and cooling it before storage is a common Indian household step and does buy time.
Sealed against odours and moisture; bring it back to room temperature before opening so condensation does not clump it.
Unopened tins and jars keep on the shelf to the printed date. The paste separates — a layer of oil on top is normal and is part of how the jar is preserved.

Refrigerate after opening and keep the oil layer covering the paste; that seal is what keeps the dried shrimp and fish in it from going rancid. Use a clean dry spoon, and smooth the surface flat again afterwards. The oil sets solid in the fridge — stand the jar out for a few minutes before scooping.
Loosely wrapped at room temperature. The layers go leathery within a day - reheat dry in a pan rather than a microwave.
Freeze plain and unfilled; a shaobing filled with egg or beef is a made-up meal and should be refrigerated and eaten the same day instead.

NCHFP gives dried vegetables roughly half the life of dried fruit — about 6 months at 60 °F (16 °C) and 3 months at 80 °F (27 °C); Ohio State's pantry table gives dried vegetables a year at 70 °F. Japan's MAFF says to keep dried goods away from heat, direct sun and damp, in a tightly sealed container.
Worth doing in a humid climate: the caps go soft and mould once they take up moisture.

Ohio State gives mushrooms 1 to 2 days in the refrigerator and says not to wash them before storing. Shiitake are firmer and drier than a button mushroom and generally hold longer; keep them gills-down in a paper bag, never sealed plastic, which sweats them.
MAFF's home vegetable freezing guide gives about 3 weeks. Slice, bag flat and freeze raw; cook from frozen.
Keep the cluster intact on its base until you cook it, in the original pack or a paper bag.

Dried block belacan and terasi are among the driest, saltiest things in an Asian pantry, and the FDA's labelling guidance lists salt and low water activity (aw 0.85 or below) as barriers that do the same job refrigeration does. A wrapped block keeps in a cool dry cupboard; wrap it in several layers or a lidded jar, because the smell travels through anything thinner. Wet paste in a jar is a different, moister product and should follow the jar's own after-opening instruction.

Refrigerate opened wet paste. Keep the surface flat and use a clean dry spoon; water introduced on a wet spoon is what starts mould. Colour deepening from pink-grey to near-black over time is normal ageing.

MHLW's tofu HACCP guide gives 絹ごし豆腐 (silken, cut and packed) a use-by of roughly 3 days and 充填豆腐 (poured into the tub, sealed, then heated) roughly 7 days, both refrigerated at 10 °C or below. Sealed-pack tofu keeps to the printed date only while unopened.
Once the seal is broken the pasteurised interior is exposed. Cover with fresh cold water in a lidded box and use within a day or two.

Sealed, to the printed date, at 0–5 °C. Skyr is technically a fresh cheese — strained hard enough to be about three times the protein of yoghurt — but it is cultured, acidic and pasteurised, and it behaves like yoghurt in the fridge. Ohio State gives yoghurt 7 to 10 days.
Keep the lid on and use a clean spoon; the low pH holds bacteria off but not mould. Weeping whey is normal, not spoilage.
It goes grainy on thawing. Fine stirred into a smoothie or a batter, wrong for eating with a spoon.
Keep whole and un-rinsed on ice at 4C or below; the skin loses its pink bloom within hours of cleaning.
Freeze whole with the head on; cleaned rings weep and go rubbery.

A whole uncut sobrasada in its casing hangs in a cool, dry, ventilated place, which is how it is made and matured on Mallorca. It stays soft and spreadable because of the fat, not because it is underdone — the cure and the paprika do the work. Keep it below about 20 °C; in a warm kitchen the fat weeps out and the surface goes rancid.

Once cut, refrigerate at or below 40 °F (4 °C) with the cut face covered. Cold sobrasada is stiff — cut what you need and let it warm before spreading, or melt it straight onto hot bread. A darkened, dried skin on the cut face can be scraped back; a sour or solvent smell means the fat has gone.
Freezing works, badly. The emulsion breaks and the thawed paste is greasy and grainy — fine stirred into a stew, poor on toast.

Cut face down on a wooden board, or in a paper bag or a cloth — not in plastic. A study that stored bread in plastic bags, paper bags and bread boxes found the paper bag held the lowest humidity (80.5 %) and the latest mould, first visible at day 5 or 6, while the plastic bag held 89.9 % and showed mould from day 4 or 5. A thick-crusted sourdough loaf holds its own moisture and the acidity of the leaven slows mould further, which is why a whole loaf outlasts a sliced one by days.

No. The same study measured a mixed-type sourdough firming to 398 % of its initial value over 10 days at 8.2 °C against 330 % at 21.9 °C — refrigeration made it noticeably staler than leaving it on the counter did. The fridge is only defensible for bread destined for the toaster.

Freeze it the day it cools, sliced, in a sealed bag. Or freeze half the loaf whole and refresh it from frozen in a 200 °C oven for 20 minutes — the crust comes back properly, which it never does from a slice.
CTAHR: the fruit softens 4 to 7 days after harvest and then has a shelf life of another 3 to 5 days. Handle gently — the skin bruises easily.
Only refrigerate once it has softened; chilling a hard fruit stops it ripening.
Freeze the sieved pulp; this is how soursop is normally kept for juice and ice cream.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial soy sauce and teriyaki sauce are safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.

Keep dry and cold in a vented bag or lidded box; never store them wet. Sprouts are grown warm and damp, which is also ideal for Salmonella and E. coli, so cook soybean sprouts thoroughly rather than eating them raw.
Storage temperatures below 50 degrees (as in a refrigerator) will cause the squash to spoil more rapidly.

A whole or half piece with the rind on, or an unopened vacuum pack, wrapped in paper at or below 4 °C. Speck is boned ham that is both dry-salted and cold-smoked over beech at low temperature, then matured for months — the smoke is a surface treatment and a flavour, and it contributes to preservation, but the salt and the drying are what actually make it stable.

Sliced or opened, a few days at or below 4 °C, tightly wrapped. Do not read the word 'smoked' as meaning 'cooked': cold-smoking is done at temperatures far too low to cook or pasteurise anything, which is the same fact that makes cold-smoked fish a Listeria concern. In speck, unlike in smoked salmon, the salt and the long dry cure do the safety work — but the smoke by itself does not.
Freeze it in a block rather than sliced; the fat oxidises quickly in thin slices.
These are sold frozen because the paper-thin sheets stale within hours at room temperature. Keep the block sealed; freezer burn shows up as brittle, opaque patches that tear when you roll.
Thaw the sealed pack in the fridge, not on the counter, and keep the sheets under a damp cloth once opened. Do not refreeze thawed sheets — they turn to paste.

Unopened commercial tubs keep to the printed date. Ssamjang is doenjang and gochujang blended with sesame oil, garlic, onion and sugar — sweeter, wetter and softer than either parent paste, so it does not keep as long.

Refrigerate after opening. Homemade ssamjang, which is mixed with raw garlic and spring onion and never heat-treated, is a shorter proposition — make what you will eat over a week or two and keep it cold.
Eat when the skin is dull and slightly wrinkled and the fruit is soft; the rind and the white latex near it are not eaten.
Whole fruit in a loose bag; it is non-climacteric so it will not improve after picking.

Do not leave filled buns out. TFDA’s rule is that cooked food is either eaten promptly or held above 60 °C; a bun cooling slowly on the counter sits in the growth range for Bacillus cereus and Staphylococcus aureus at once.

A cooked filled bun is a starchy food with a meat or vegetable centre — the combination Bacillus cereus favours. TFDA allows short refrigerated storage of two days or less at 5 °C or below, and requires freezing for anything longer. Steam back to a genuinely hot centre, never lukewarm.
Cool completely, wrap each bun, then freeze. Steam from frozen for 12-15 minutes; microwaving from frozen leaves a cold core.

Firmer and drier than most blues, so it keeps at the long end of the blue-cheese range: two to three weeks at 0–5 °C, cut face covered with waxed paper or foil and the rind left exposed. A whole or half truckle in its wrapper keeps longer than a cut wedge — the cut face is where it dries, browns and picks up stray moulds. In the UK the use-by date on the pack is the legal limit, so use it while the wrapper is intact.
Only for soup and sauce. It thaws crumbly and wet.

Raw stinky tofu is a fresh, high-moisture, low-acid soy product that has already been through an uncontrolled brine ferment — keep it at 4 °C or below, boxed so the smell does not transfer, and cook it through. It is not a shelf-stable preserved food.
Freeze raw pieces individually; the texture turns spongy, which suits deep-frying and braising.

Wrapped in foil or in its sealed bag, in a cool dry place — a cold larder is better than a warm kitchen. Stollen is built to keep: the baked loaf is brushed with a great deal of melted butter and then buried in caster and icing sugar, which sets into a shell that seals the surface against air and moisture, and the crumb itself is heavy with fat, sugar and soaked dried fruit. Traditionally it is baked weeks ahead and matured before Christmas, and it genuinely improves for the first fortnight.

Once cut, press the two cut halves back together and wrap the whole loaf again rather than wrapping the open faces — that is the traditional method and it works, because the sugar crust is still doing its job everywhere except at the cut. Weeks, not days.
Not the fridge — it stales the crumb and makes the sugar crust weep. Cool and dry is what stollen wants.
Freezes whole with no harm at all. Thaw in the wrapper at room temperature so the condensation forms outside the foil rather than on the sugar.

Fresh straw mushrooms are notoriously short-lived and are actually damaged by cold storage below about 10 °C, which turns them grey and watery. Buy them the day you cook them; otherwise buy the canned ones.
Ripen at room temperature until the fruit gives to gentle pressure. Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture is explicit that it must not be refrigerated before it is ripe.
Refrigerate only once ripe, and eat quickly; the flesh darkens fast once chilled.
Scoop out the pulp, discard the seeds and freeze in portions.
Whole unpeeled stalks keep in a cool, shaded spot; the cut ends dry out and go fibrous first.

Peeled or chopped sections must be refrigerated and wrapped. Discard any cane whose pith has gone reddish-brown or smells sour or alcoholic rather than sweet - mould in stored cane is the reason to be fussy here.

Airtight, dark, dry, away from heat — Ohioline's 6 months for ground spices. Sumac is the clearest case in the spice rack of colour telling you the truth: fresh sumac is deep wine-red and tastes sharply lemony; faded brick-brown sumac has lost the acid and tastes only salty. Many brands are salted, which does nothing for keeping quality. It clumps in a humid kitchen because the ground berry is slightly moist and sticky by nature.

The vinegar is a control measure, not a decoration. Hong Kong’s CFS requires sushi rice to be acidified to pH 4.6 or below, which holds back Bacillus cereus and Staphylococcus aureus while the rice sits at working temperature. Properly acidified rice may be held at room temperature for a working session, but unacidified rice may not.

MHLW’s guide for school-meal rice — which explicitly covers rice with vinegar or other ingredients mixed in after cooking — says cooked rice must not be carried over past the day it was made, and that stored rice goes above 55 °C or below 8 °C for as short a time as possible. Chilled sushi rice goes hard and crumbly; let it warm up before use.
